# Distribution & Business-Model Architecture: Climate-Linked Microinsurance for Smallholders (2026 Pilot)

*A decision-ready framework covering channel strategy, claim credibility, and portfolio construction across East Africa, South Asia, and Central America.*

---

## Core Principle

A microinsurance policy is not a document that gets distributed — it is a **promise that gets believed**. What is being sold is not coverage but *confidence in a future payout*: a wallet notification in Nakuru, a cash envelope at a co-op assembly in Huehuetenango, a SHG meeting announcement in Bihar.

Two failure modes to avoid: shipping one global product with translated brochures, and running three disconnected pilots that can't pool risk or share data infrastructure. The architecture that works is two-layered:

- **Layer 1 — Global Risk & Integrity Core (non-negotiable, centrally owned):** parametric product standards, data-quality floors, pre-funded claims accounts, reinsurance structure, trigger transparency, fraud controls. Identical everywhere.
- **Layer 2 — Regional Trust & Distribution Layer (regionally owned):** lead intermediary, positioning, payment rails, payout rituals, premium collection mechanics. Radically different by region.

**In microinsurance, the claim is the product — the policy is just the receipt.** The first payout in a village is the entire marketing budget; the first *denied* payout is the entire reputational write-down. Acquisition cost is a trust problem, claim credibility is a data problem, and portfolio risk is a correlation problem — design for each separately.

---

## 1. Three Trust Regimes

| | **East Africa** (Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Rwanda) | **South Asia** (India, Bangladesh; Nepal/Pakistan later) | **Central America** (Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador — Dry Corridor) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Baseline trust in formal insurance** | Low; a decade of index pilots (some failed payouts) left "insurance doesn't pay" folklore | Low-moderate; PMFBY created mass awareness *and* mass cynicism about multi-season claim delays | Very low; insurance perceived as a product for the urban rich; bank and state distrust spill over |
| **Most legitimate intermediaries** | M-Pesa agents, SACCOs/dairy co-ops, agrovet input dealers, lead farmers | Women's SHGs, MFIs, Farmer Producer Organizations, CSC operators; NGO field networks (Bangladesh) | Coffee co-ops, Catholic parishes and evangelical churches, remittance agents, savings groups |
| **Payment rails** | Mobile money ubiquitous — payout can be instant | UPI/Aadhaar (India), bKash/Nagad (Bangladesh) — strong and cheap | Cash-dominant; mobile money thin; remittance outlets are the trusted cash-in/cash-out network |
| **Claim-speed expectation** | Instant — the mobile-money norm; speed is the baseline, not a differentiator | Slow is expected (state scheme delays measured in months) — *beating it is the differentiator* | Undefined; payout at a known, trusted window matters more than raw speed |
| **Actuarial data quality** | Good satellite record (CHIRPS), growing station networks (TAHMO); sparse ground truth in arid zones | Dense stations in India; strong flood/cyclone modeling in Bangladesh; contested area-yield data | Sparse stations, mountain microclimates; satellite-dependent; weakest of the three |
| **Dominant perils** | Drought, erratic onset, dry spells (livestock adjacent) | Monsoon flood, drought, cyclone (coastal Bangladesh) | Drought and canícula failure, excess rain, hurricane (Caribbean slope) |
| **Regulatory posture** | Microinsurance windows and sandboxes (e.g., Kenya IRA) | IRDAI microinsurance framework; PMFBY ecosystem to navigate; takaful demand in Bangladesh | Thin microinsurance regulation; fronting via licensed local insurers required; ring-fence Nicaragua (political/regulatory risk) |
| **The trust question the farmer asks** | *"Will the money actually land on my phone when the rains fail?"* | *"Will I be paid faster than the government scheme — and is my name on the list?"* | *"Who do I know that stands behind this?"* |

*Note: sovereign and meso-level schemes (African Risk Capacity, CCRIF, PMFBY) are complements, not competitors — design micro products to stack underneath their triggers, and position as gap-cover where a state scheme exists.*

---

## 2. Intermediary Scorecard

| Channel | Trust legitimacy | Reach & density | Acquisition cost profile | Claim-credibility contribution | Principal risks | Portfolio-shape effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cooperatives** | High — member-owned, existing ledgers | Medium; dense in cash-crop zones (dairy, coffee) | **Lowest**: group enrollment at general assemblies; near-zero marginal cost per member | High — peer witnessing of payouts; co-op attestation as verification layer | Leadership capture; co-mingling of premiums; covariate concentration (one watershed, one crop) | Correlated clusters — cap per co-op |
| **Mobile-network agents** | Medium-high in East Africa (agent is a known neighbor); lower elsewhere | **Highest** national reach | Moderate: commissions; must pay on *renewal*, not just sale | **Highest when payout is instant to wallet** — the demonstration effect is self-propagating | Mis-selling, agent fraud, liquidity shortfalls, churn incentives | Nationally dispersed — best diversifier |
| **Religious community groups** | **Highest** in Central America (churches) and Muslim-majority South Asia (mosques; takaful fit) | Medium; weekly gathering rhythm | Very low: endorsement + assembly enrollment | Moral guarantee of the leader — powerful but

Distribution candidates include cooperatives, mobile-network agents, religious community groups, and fintech apps. Trust in formal insurance, expectations of claim speed, and the perceived legitimacy of different intermediaries vary greatly by region, and actuarial data quality is uneven.
